Carrot Top Awake and Breathing on His Own After Hospitalization Following Reported Suicide Attempt

Scott Thompson, the comedian known as Carrot Top, was hospitalized on Friday, September 18, following what TMZ described as a suicide attempt. By September 20, his publicist confirmed he was awake, breathing on his own, and had been sharing moments of humor with the medical staff treating him – a detail that offered the first specific sign of progress since the crisis began.

Advertisements

His publicist, Jami Schlicher, told USA TODAY that Thompson had shared “moments of humor with the medical staff caring for him,” adding that humor “has always been such an important part of who Scott is.” Many messages from fans had been shared with Thompson, including stories about how his comedy helped them through difficult periods in their own lives. His family and those closest to him remain deeply grateful for the support and continue to ask that his privacy be respected.

Carrot Top was allegedly being extorted over a sex tape before his apparent suicide attempt.

Thompson was hospitalized Friday, Sept. 18, in what TMZ described as a suicide attempt. His representative confirmed the hospitalization and his recovery, but has not publicly confirmed that it was a suicide attempt or disclosed what led to the medical emergency. TMZ’s characterization is treated here as a reported suicide attempt pending further confirmation.

Fox News reported that an MGM Resorts spokesperson said: “Scott is a beloved member of the Luxor and MGM Resorts family, and we are relieved to hear that he is recovering. We are thinking of him and wish him strength as he receives the care and support he needs.”

Advertisements

Schlicher’s statement on Sept. 20 offered the first real-time recovery detail since the crisis began two days earlier. She noted that hearing fan stories and feeling their support “has meant a great deal to him during his recovery,” and that he and his family “remain deeply grateful for the extraordinary kindness.”

A career built on four decades of laughter

Thompson’s stand-up career began in the late 1980s. He appeared on Star Search in 1991, a platform that helped expand his national profile. His act is built around prop comedy – multicolor outfits, a mane of red hair, and a seemingly endless supply of custom-made inventions and gags pulled from large trunks on stage. Each prop must be designed, built, tested, and timed, and Thompson developed one of the most recognizable acts in American stand-up around that format.

He built his national profile further through college-tour bookings in the early 1990s, where his prop-heavy act translated effectively to large audiences. After landing a guest spot on The Tonight Show with Jay Leno in 1992, Thompson gained a broader fan base. Comedy Central specials followed. The stage persona he developed during that period – big energy, rapid-fire delivery, physical comedy anchored by absurdist objects – became a fixture in American stand-up.

Advertisements

He was also, for much of that time, a figure who attracted as much criticism as fans. “If you read what people say about you, it will kill you,” he told Esquire in 2015. “I’ve always been love or hate,” he said. “That’s fine. Thank God I’ve had more love than hate.”

The Luxor residency and what’s now at stake

Thompson has held a prop-comedy residency at the Luxor Hotel & Casino since November 22, 2005 – one of the longest-tenured residencies in Las Vegas history. During a September 2025 appearance on The Joe Rogan Experience, Thompson spoke about the “great advantage” of having the Las Vegas residency. “I’m home at 10:30, 11 at the latest,” he said. “You can have a normal day.”

MGM Resorts, which operates the Luxor, canceled Thompson’s Friday and Saturday performances after his hospitalization. The residency is normally dark on Sundays. A Monday show was also canceled, leaving ticketholders for multiple nights without performances.

Advertisements

The pressure building before the crisis

In the period before September 18, Thompson was facing mounting legal pressure. Singer Brian Evans, a former Carrot Top opening act, filed a federal lawsuit against Thompson alleging Thompson had sent Evans an unsolicited sexually explicit video. Thompson did not publicly address the suit. No connection between the litigation and the reported suicide attempt has been confirmed by Thompson’s team.

A legal declaration connected to a separate proceeding alleged that Thompson was seen at a bar around 2 p.m. on Friday, hours before his show was set to begin at 8 p.m.

His former fellow prop comedian Gallagher died in November 2022 at age 76. The two had a complicated relationship that included a notable falling-out before Gallagher’s death.

Advertisements

Thompson had also, in recent years, spoken more openly about childhood experiences that shaped him. He endured significant bullying while growing up in Florida, primarily because of his distinctive appearance. His red hair, which became the centerpiece of his stage persona, was also the source of years of cruelty when he was young. His father was a NASA engineer.

What the 988 Lifeline data shows about crisis support

Suicide resulted in more than 49,000 deaths in the U.S. in 2023, a figure that is up 31% from 2003, according to a 2026 U.S. Government Accountability Office report. The same report noted that crisis intervention infrastructure has expanded significantly in response. About 19.1 million calls, texts, and chats were routed to crisis contact centers from July 2022 through September 2025, with call volume increasing by about 87 percent and text volume by about 260 percent during that period.

From July 2022 through December 2024, suicide deaths among people ages 15 to 34 were 11% lower than projected rates based on pre-988 trends, representing approximately 4,372 lives saved. Reductions were significantly greater in the 10 states with the highest uptake in 988 calls, according to analysis published by the Pew Charitable Trusts.

Advertisements

In 2024, suicide and substance-related deaths combined were the third leading cause of death in the U.S., behind heart disease and cancer, according to KFF.

The 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline – reachable by calling or texting 988, or by chatting at 988lifeline.org – connects callers to trained counselors, 24 hours a day. It is free, confidential, and available across the United States. For people who prefer text, messaging “HELLO” to 741741 connects to the Crisis Text Line.

What comes next

Thompson remains in the hospital as of the most recent update on September 20. His family is with him. Schlicher’s statement was more hopeful than the silence that preceded it – an update shaped, almost certainly, by a man who still, even in recovery, led with a joke.

Advertisements

The Luxor has expressed relief and support. The broader Las Vegas entertainment community, which has watched Thompson headline the same stage for over two decades, is watching. The question of when Thompson steps back onto that stage – and whether performing will continue to anchor his life the way it has for more than 40 years – belongs entirely to him and to the people who are caring for him now.

If you or someone you know is struggling, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, available 24 hours a day, seven days a week. You can also text “HELLO” to 741741 to reach the Crisis Text Line.
